messages.subject: location-scale "mat trick" for multivariate normal
parts:
The FAQ for improving speed suggests to reduce correlations in posterior draws for higher-level hyperparameters under a multivariate Gaussian by drawing from from multi_normal() using a correlation matrix with location = 0 and then scaling and locating the result.   Suppose one has a matrix[T,D] delta where delta[t] ~ multi_normal(fred,S) for D x D covariance, S.   Would it be better  to draw a T x D matrix of standard normals, Z, and scale each row_vector, z[t], by the cholesky decomposition of S and then add mean, fred?   i suppose we avoid forming S under the suggested process, however, but such seems a small cost, given the correlation matrix and scale vector.  i know (from Ben) that even better is to directly update lp_ with the quadratic product kernel of the Gaussian.  maybe take the cholesky decomposition of the covariance matrix and compute the inverse of that in the absence of having gaussian elimination available.   i'd like to first get the simpler approach working, however.

--
Thank you, Terrance Savitsky

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: location-scale "mat trick" for multivariate normal
parts:
On Monday, October 15, 2012 9:40:11 PM UTC-4, tds151 wrote:
The FAQ for improving speed suggests to reduce correlations in posterior draws for higher-level hyperparameters under a multivariate Gaussian by drawing from from multi_normal() using a correlation matrix with location = 0 and then scaling and locating the result.   Suppose one has a matrix[T,D] delta where delta[t] ~ multi_normal(fred,S) for D x D covariance, S.   Would it be better  to draw a T x D matrix of standard normals, Z, and scale each row_vector, z[t], by the cholesky decomposition of S and then add mean, fred?   i suppose we avoid forming S under the suggested process, however, but such seems a small cost, given the correlation matrix and scale vector.  i know (from Ben) that even better is to directly update lp_ with the quadratic product kernel of the Gaussian.  maybe take the cholesky decomposition of the covariance matrix and compute the inverse of that in the absence of having gaussian elimination available.   i'd like to first get the simpler approach working, however.

If S were known, then you could do both the Matt trick and update the log-posterior without explicitly calling the multi_normal() function, which is currently not very optimized. If S were a parameter, then things are more involved. In

for (t in 1:T) {
 row(delta,t) ~ multi_normal(fred,S);
}

it is essentially going to invert the S matrix T times, so you want to avoid that. Hopefully, you will be able to do delta ~ multi_normal(fred,S) in the next version or two of Stan.

In the meantime, I think your suggestion about a Cholesky factor could work.

parameters {
  cov_matrix[D] S;
  vector[D] fred;
  matrix[T,D] Z;
  ...
}
transformed parameters {
  matrix[T,D] delta;
  matrix[D,D] L;
  L <- cholesky_decompose(S);
  // Multivariate Matt trick
  for (t in 1:T) {
    col(delta,t) <- fred + L * col(Z,t);
  }
}
model {
  // rows or columns of Z are iid standard normal
  // use delta in your loglikelihood
}

Or you could make L the parameter instead of S to avoid the cholesky_decompose(), but it is harder to choose a prior on L. I suppose you could make S a transformed parameter and put a prior on S, but then you have to make a manual Jacobian adjustment for the change-of-variables.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: location-scale "mat trick" for multivariate normal
parts:
As always, thank you.  I've bumped into a compiler error that I believe may be a stan-level bug related to this trick, so I report it here.

transformed parameters {
// some declarations and set-up
        cov_matrix[D] S_t; 
        matrix[D,D] L_t;
        L_t          <- cholesky_decompose(S_t);

       // this doesn't pass compilation - I'm assuming Delta[t] is of type row_vector, but it is not.
       // the stan syntax checker, however, appears to recognize Delta[t] as a row_vector, though the compiler is unable to perform the assignment.
       matrix[T,D] Delta;
       for( t in 1:T ) Delta[t] <- (L_t * Delta_norm[t]')';

      // this does pass compilation.
      row_vector[D] Delta[T];
       for( t in 1:T ) Delta[t] <- (L_t * Delta_norm[t]')';
}

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: location-scale "mat trick" for multivariate normal
parts:
On Tuesday, October 16, 2012 5:42:38 PM UTC-4, tds151 wrote:
As always, thank you.  I've bumped into a compiler error that I believe may be a stan-level bug related to this trick, so I report it here.

transformed parameters {
// some declarations and set-up
        cov_matrix[D] S_t; 
        matrix[D,D] L_t;
        L_t          <- cholesky_decompose(S_t);

       // this doesn't pass compilation - I'm assuming Delta[t] is of type row_vector, but it is not.
       // the stan syntax checker, however, appears to recognize Delta[t] as a row_vector, though the compiler is unable to perform the assignment.
       matrix[T,D] Delta;
       for( t in 1:T ) Delta[t] <- (L_t * Delta_norm[t]')';
You need row(Delta, t) <- SomeRowVector;

// this does pass compilation.
      row_vector[D] Delta[T];
       for( t in 1:T ) Delta[t] <- (L_t * Delta_norm[t]')';
}

I think that is legal, but surveys have shown that exactly 50% of people find this confusing. The other 50% finds it intuitive.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: matrix & row index produces a row vector?
parts:
On 10/16/12 8:36 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Tuesday, October 16, 2012 5:42:38 PM UTC-4, tds151 wrote:

> I think that is legal, but surveys have shown that exactly 50% of people find this confusing. The other 50% finds it
> intuitive.

I think that sample consists of me and Andrew.

I had thought this was a common matrix notation:

matrix[3,2] m;
row_vector[2] rv;

rv <- m[1];

but couldn't find it on Wikipedia or in Strang or
in Golub (or in MATLAB or R).

To me, it's the most natural thing in the world
to take a two-argument function x(a,b) and to
abstract (bind in C++ terms; lambda abstraction
in function programming terms) the second argument.
Then x(a) is the function that when applied to be
produces x(a,b).

I won't repeat what Andrew said, but let's just say
he's not in favor of that notation.

This is like learning that an expression you've used your
whole life turns out to be a regional colloquialism
and not the Queen's English!

- Bob

I'm one of the 50% (or is that now 66%?) that find this syntax somewhat confusing and ambigious.  In Matlab m[1]  corresponds to direct linear indexing into a column major array of the matrix and will return a scalar value.

My syntactic preference is for something a bit more explicit.  I.E.,

matrix[3,2] m;
  row_vector[2] rv;

rv <- m[1,:];

That way you can also do

  vector[3] cv;

  cv <- m[:,1];

Python and Matlab both do something like this.

Queen's English indeed ;)

Cheers,
Marcus
